title: Stochastic Optimization with Random Search
claim: The proposed method fails with tiny batches but, as batch size grows, converges faster and more stably than baselines.
layout: 6 panels, 2x3 grid, one per batch size, shared legend
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots, each showing objective f(x) on the y-axis against function queries (up to 2.1×10^5) on the x-axis. Panels are labeled beneath as (a) b=1, (b) b=5, (c) b=10, (d) b=25, (e) b=50 and (f) b=100. Each panel plots three methods: Mi2P as a solid blue line with a shaded band, RSGF as an orange dashed line, and ZO-CD as a green dotted line. All curves drop sharply from about 0.65 and then flatten. In (a), Mi2P plateaus near 0.19 with a wide noisy band, well above the baselines. In (b), Mi2P roughly matches them. From (c) to (f), Mi2P drops fastest and stays lowest, and its lead over the baselines grows with batch size. The eye goes first to the steep initial drops and the blue curve.
caption: Breast Cancer (logistic): f(x) vs. queries for different batch sizes. Mean ± one s.d. across 20 runs.
abstract: We revisit random search for stochastic optimization, where only noisy function evaluations are available. We show that the method works under weaker smoothness assumptions than previously considered, and that stronger assumptions enable improved guarantees. In the finite-sum setting, we design a variance-reduced variant that leverages multiple samples to accelerate convergence. Our analysis relies on a simple translation invariance property, which provides a principled way to balance noise and reduce variance.
